body: Three frameworks govern lab animal work. The Animal Welfare Act (AWA) is LAW, enforced by USDA-APHIS through unannounced inspections; it excludes purpose-bred rats, mice, and birds. The PHS Policy, administered by OLAW (NIH), is a funding condition that requires institutions to follow the Guide and covers ALL vertebrates. AAALAC International is a private, VOLUNTARY accreditation. FDA's Good Laboratory Practice (GLP, 21 CFR 58) governs safety studies. USDA pain categories: B (bred/held), C (no/minimal pain), D (pain RELIEVED with drugs), E (pain UNRELIEVED — needs scientific justification). Remember: AWA = law/USDA; PHS = policy/OLAW; AAALAC = voluntary gold standard.

The IACUC oversees the institution's animal program. Membership minimum: 3 under the AWA, 5 under PHS Policy — always including a veterinarian, a nonaffiliated member, and (PHS) a nonscientist. The committee must review the program and inspect every animal facility at least every 6 months (semiannually). Protocols can be approved by Designated Member Review (DMR) OR Full Committee Review (FCR); any member may call any protocol to FCR. To SUSPEND an activity requires a majority vote of a quorum at a convened meeting. The Institutional Official (IO) holds ultimate authority and reports suspensions to USDA/OLAW.

Russell and Burch (1959) defined the 3Rs, the ethical foundation of humane animal use. REPLACEMENT: use non-animal methods (in vitro, computer models) or less-sentient organisms instead of animals. REDUCTION: use the fewest animals needed for valid results — through good statistics and design. REFINEMENT: modify husbandry and procedures to minimize pain and distress and enhance welfare (better analgesia, enrichment, training). The IACUC weighs the 3Rs in every protocol. Hook: Replace, Reduce, Refine — fewer animals, less suffering, no-animal alternatives first.

The MACROenvironment is the room; the MICROenvironment is inside the cage. Key Guide targets for rodents: relative humidity 30–70%, ventilation roughly 10–15 air changes per hour, a 12:12 light cycle, and illumination around 325 lux at cage level to protect albino retinas. Keep noise low (sustained noise above ~85 dB and ultrasonic sources stress rodents). Temperature ranges are species-specific. Low humidity predisposes rats to ringtail; high humidity drives ammonia and microbial growth. The goal is a stable, species-appropriate environment that supports normal physiology and reproducible science.

The primary enclosure (cage) creates the microenvironment the animal actually experiences — its air quality, temperature, and humidity. The Guide specifies minimum floor area and cage HEIGHT by species and body weight (e.g., mice need ≥5 in height). Static (filter-top) cages rely on room air and need frequent changing; individually ventilated cages (IVC) deliver HEPA-filtered air to each cage, improving intracage air quality, extending change intervals, and boosting biosecurity. Whatever the system, the microenvironment — not just the room — must meet the animals' needs.

Three escalating levels: SANITIZE (reduce microbes to safe levels — routine cage washing), DISINFECT (kill most pathogens, maybe not spores), STERILIZE (destroy ALL microbial life including spores). Cage-wash final rinse should reach at least 180°F (82.2°C). Steam autoclaving sterilizes at 121°C, 15 psi, for 15+ minutes. Verify sterilizers with biological indicators — Geobacillus stearothermophilus spores for steam. Static rodent cages are typically sanitized at least every 2 weeks; soiled bedding drives ammonia, so monitor and change on a performance basis.

Know your air and your cabinets. POSITIVE pressure rooms push air out to protect clean/immunocompromised animals; NEGATIVE pressure rooms pull air in to CONTAIN hazards (infectious agents, quarantine). Biosafety cabinets: Class I protects worker + environment (not product); Class II protects worker + product + environment (the workhorse for biologicals); Class III is a fully sealed glovebox for the most dangerous agents. A chemical FUME HOOD protects the worker from vapors but does NOT protect product and does NOT filter biologicals. Facilities also need security and disaster/contingency plans.

Diet types: natural-ingredient (agricultural products), purified (refined ingredients), and chemically defined (pure chemicals). Processing options include certified (contaminant-tested), autoclavable (fortified to survive heat), and irradiated. Standard rodent chow is generally used within ~6 months of the MILLING date because vitamins — especially vitamin C and A — degrade. Guinea pigs and primates cannot make vitamin C, so their feed needs fresh ascorbic acid and short shelf life. Store feed cool, dry, off the floor, and rotate stock first-in/first-out.

Daily husbandry sustains animal welfare and science. QUARANTINE separates incoming animals to detect disease before it reaches the colony; ACCLIMATION lets animals stabilize physiologically after shipping before use. Identify animals reliably (cage cards, ear tags/punches, tattoos, microchips) and keep accurate records. Provide ENRICHMENT (nesting material for mice, gnaw items, social housing for social species) to promote species-typical behavior. SPF = Specific Pathogen Free, meaning free of a DEFINED list of pathogens — not necessarily germ-free. Observe every animal daily for health and report abnormalities.

Mice (Mus musculus): gestation ~19–21 days, weaning ~21 days, with a fertile POSTPARTUM estrus right after birth. Social animals — group house and give nesting material. Three pheromone effects to know: WHITTEN (male pheromone synchronizes/induces female estrus), BRUCE (a strange male's pheromone blocks early pregnancy), LEE-BOOT (grouped females without a male suppress estrus / become pseudopregnant). Strains may be inbred (isogenic) or outbred. Handle gently — tunnel or cupped-hand handling reduces stress versus tail handling.

Rats (Rattus norvegicus): gestation ~21–23 days, social and intelligent. Two classic anatomy facts: rats have NO gallbladder and CANNOT vomit (so they can't expel toxins — relevant to toxicology). RINGTAIL (annular tail constrictions) is linked to LOW humidity. Red-tinged tears/nasal discharge is CHROMODACRYORRHEA — porphyrin from the Harderian gland, a stress/illness sign, NOT blood. Common stocks include Sprague-Dawley and Wistar (outbred) and inbred strains like F344. Handle confidently and support the body.

Small rodents differ sharply. SYRIAN HAMSTERS are solitary/territorial (house singly), have cheek pouches, hibernate-prone in cold, and the shortest gestation (~16 days). GERBILS are social (bonded pairs), have a ventral abdominal scent gland, and are prone to spontaneous epileptiform SEIZURES when startled. GUINEA PIGS need dietary VITAMIN C (cannot synthesize it), are born precocial (furred, eyes open), have a long gestation (~59–72 days), and are prone to dystocia if first bred after the pubic symphysis fuses (~6–8 months).

Rabbits (Oryctolagus cuniculus) are INDUCED ovulators — mating triggers ovulation, no regular cycle. They practice CECOTROPHY (re-ingesting nutrient-rich night feces) and cannot vomit, so GI STASIS is a serious emergency. They absorb dietary calcium efficiently and excrete the excess in urine (cloudy/chalky urine is normal). 'SNUFFLES' (upper respiratory disease) is classically Pasteurella multocida. RESTRAINT: always support the hindquarters — a kick with an unsupported spine can fracture lumbar vertebrae and cause paralysis.

Nonhuman primates demand strict safety. HERPES B VIRUS (Macacine herpesvirus 1) is usually silent in macaques but frequently FATAL in humans after bites, scratches, or mucosal splashes — wear full PPE (mask, face shield, gloves). TB is a major concern: test by intradermal tuberculin in the upper EYELID (palpebral), read at 24/48/72 h. New arrivals get a quarantine of at least ~6 weeks. NHPs are highly social — provide social housing and psychological enrichment. Many agents are zoonotic in BOTH directions, so personnel health screening matters.

Beyond rodents and rabbits: DOGS require an AWA-mandated exercise plan and benefit from socialization. CATS need elevated resting and litter. NONHUMAN-care aside, SWINE are used in cardiovascular/skin research. FERRETS are obligate carnivores used in influenza/neuroscience work. AGRICULTURAL species (ruminants, swine) in biomedical research follow the Guide; in agricultural research, the Ag Guide applies. Aquatic and exotic species (zebrafish, Xenopus, birds, reptiles) have specialized water-quality, temperature, and humidity needs. Match husbandry to the species' natural biology.

Protect the people. LABORATORY ANIMAL ALLERGY (LAA) is the most common occupational health problem — allergens come from animal URINE, dander, and saliva (rodent urinary proteins are major), and can progress to asthma. Control exposure using the HIERARCHY OF CONTROLS: elimination/substitution > ENGINEERING controls (ventilated change stations, IVC) > administrative controls (practices, training) > PPE (last line). Know ZOONOSES (Herpes B, rat-bite fever, Q fever, LCMV) and keep vaccinations (tetanus, rabies where indicated) current. Enroll all animal handlers in the occupational health program.

INBRED strains come from 20+ generations of brother-sister mating — animals are isogenic (genetically identical) and homozygous; great for reproducibility. OUTBRED stocks are deliberately genetically variable, modeling population diversity. Cross two inbred strains and you get uniform F1 HYBRIDS (heterozygous, often with hybrid vigor). CONGENIC strains are made by repeated backcrossing to move a single locus onto an inbred background. TRANSGENIC animals carry an inserted foreign gene; KNOCKOUTS have a gene inactivated. Standardized nomenclature (e.g., C57BL/6J) precisely identifies strain and substrain.

Anesthesia abolishes sensation so procedures are humane. ISOFLURANE is a volatile INHALANT delivered by precision vaporizer — fast induction/recovery and easy depth control make it ideal for rodents. Monitor DEPTH continuously: loss of the PEDAL WITHDRAWAL reflex (firm toe pinch with no limb withdrawal) signals a surgical plane. Also watch respiratory rate/pattern, mucous-membrane color, and body temperature (anesthetized rodents lose heat fast — use supplemental warmth). Distinguish anesthesia (unconsciousness + analgesia) from analgesia (pain relief) and from paralytics (no anesthesia at all).

Follow the AVMA Guidelines for the Euthanasia of Animals (2020). For rodents, CO2 from a compressed gas cylinder with a GRADUAL fill of about 30–70% of chamber volume per minute is standard — never pre-fill with 100% CO2. ALWAYS confirm death and apply a SECONDARY method (cervical dislocation, decapitation, or confirming no heartbeat) before disposal, since animals can recover if removed early. Cervical dislocation without sedation is acceptable for mice and for rats under ~200 g. The method must be appropriate to species, age, and the science.

Core techniques: injection routes are SC (under skin), IM (muscle), IP (abdominal cavity), and IV (vein) — each has volume limits and a preferred site. ORAL GAVAGE delivers an exact dose to the stomach via a feeding tube. Blood: total volume is ~7–8% of body weight; remove no more than ~10% at one time in a healthy animal, allowing weeks to recover. Controlled drugs follow DEA schedules (I–V) with strict logging. Practice good experimental DESIGN (controls, randomization, adequate n) and be fluent in metric unit conversions for accurate dosing.
